content: WFXRtv Stopping Dengue and other mosquito-borne illnesses Nicholas Noleff 3 days ago ROANOKE, Va. (WFXR) – Dengue virus is a mosquito-borne illness that is normally found within tropical and sub-tropical areas. “Dengue viruses are spread to people through the bites of infected Aedes species mosquitoes,” says Dr. Julia Murphy, the State Public Health Veterinarian for the Virginia Department of Health. Mosquitos are considered vectors, meaning they’re organisms that can transmit diseases like dengue. “The one that spreads dengue the most efficiently and is considered the primary vector, if you will, of dengue virus is called Aedes Aegypti.” The species is native to Africa, but has appeared in the U.S. sporadically over the years as an invasive species. But, the U.S. is home to another species of Aedes mosquito; Aedes Albopictus. “The kind of Aedes mosquito that we have in abundance, is one that is a competent vector, you could say, but it’s really not the main driver of dengue,” says Murphy. “It has a tendency to have a broader array of animals that it bites.” According to the World Health Organization, up to 400 million people around the world are at risk of becoming infected with dengue each year. But unlike other viruses that spread from person to person, dengue spreads through mosquito bites. “You have a person who’s infected with dengue, a person for whom dengue virus is circulating in their blood, a mosquito vector mosquito bites that person, “says Murphy. “Then after a relatively short period of time, that mosquito becomes infected with the dengue virus, and then if that mosquito bites another person, then that person gets infected.” Earlier this month, VDH confirmed the first case of dengue to be locally acquired here in Virginia. “We had a person in Northern Virginia who tested positive for the dengue virus and it appears that that infection was locally acquired, which means that person got infected in Virginia,” says Murphy. However, health officials say while this case is historic, it’s not unprecedented. “Over the years, 2010 through 2025, of all of the dengue virus infections that were reported as happening in people in the United States about 95% of them were travel associated,” says Murphy. VDH says while other potentially locally acquired cases are possible, it’s unlikely to see other cases at this time. “A lot of times that people at highest risk for additional transmission are folks in the household or folks who are in close proximity to a person with dengue virus in circulation,” says Murphy. Not everyone will have a reaction to the virus, as some people can appear asymptomatic to the infection. “Dengue can have a wide clinical spectrum that can occur,” says Murphy. “A lot of people don’t become sick at all.” However, for those that are impacted by the disease, symptoms can vary. “Oftentimes they’ll get a fever, that’s a real hallmark of dengue,” says Murphy. “Then they have general aches and pains, sort of especially one feature of dengue can be in some people, a lot of pain behind the eyes, what’s called retro ball pain.” Other symptoms can include nausea, vomiting, muscle and joint pain, and a skin rash. “A smaller subset, probably around five-percent of people, can get what’s called severe dengue,” says Murphy. “As the name would suggest, that is a severe illness that can result in things like shock and internal bleeding.” But while the risk of dengue spreading in the Commonwealth isn’t large, there are other mosquito-borne illnesses to be on the lookout for, including West Nile Virus. VDH says prevention is key, and there are plenty of tools people can use to not only help prevent dengue, but all mosquito-born illnesses. “Some good prevention measures include things like when you’re outdoors using mosquito repellent,” says Murphy. “What I would say is always follow the directions on the label.” Not every repellant is able to be used by all people, which is why experts say it’s important to know what ingredients are inside before spraying it on yourself, a child, or a pet. “It’s important to look at that label and also look at the concentrations of of the various ingredients, because there are some precautions and recommendations for children,” says Murphy. “There may also be some cautions and recommendations associated with any pets you have.” Dr. Murphy suggests checking out the EPA’s website to determine which insect repellant is right for you. Another thing to utilize for protection is making sure you have screens on your windows, and that there aren’t any holes in them. “A lot of people like to have their door open or their windows open,” says Murphy. “Make sure that screen is in good repair, make sure your window screens are being repaired because you want to try to keep mosquitoes out.” Finally, it’s important to manage pools of water near your home, as stagnant water can become a breeding ground for mosquito larva. “You can help to drive down the populations of mosquitoes in and around your yard by helping to eliminate or routinely refreshing any standing water in your backyard,” says Murphy. Mosquito eggs need just seven to ten days to transition into a full-grown adult mosquito. “So if mosquitoes are laying their eggs in there and you’re disrupting that cycle at least once a week, it’ll really decrease the likelihood that any eggs that are in there would go on to become adults,” says Murphy. PC: by Wendy Osher The Hawaiʻi Department of Health has identified a new travel-related dengue virus case on Oʻahu, bringing the total number of dengue cases reported in Hawaiʻi to seven in 2026. The individual was exposed to the virus while traveling internationally in a region where dengue is common. No connection to any prior cases in Hawaiʻi has been identified. DOH teams have been deployed to conduct inspections and implement mosquito-control measures in the affected area. Due to the circumstances of this case, the expected risk of transmission is low. However, with recent flooding from Tropical Cyclone Lala and anticipated rain in the forecast, this case is a reminder for the public to eliminate standing water as much as possible. Reducing standing water helps prevent mosquito breeding and can reduce the risk of local transmission of vector-borne diseases. More information about mosquito control is available on the vector control website. Dengue virus is transmitted from an infected person to a mosquito and then to another person. While Hawaiʻi is home to mosquitoes that can carry dengue, the disease is not endemic, or established, in the state; cases are currently limited to travelers. Of the seven dengue cases reported in Hawaiʻi in 2026, all have involved travel to Pacific island countries and territories. Dengue is a year-round risk in tropical and subtropical areas of Central and South America, including Brazil and Mexico; Asia, including the Philippines; the Middle East; Africa; and several Pacific islands, including American Samoa, the Federated States of Micronesia, the Republic of the Marshall Islands and the Republic of Palau. Many popular tourist destinations in the Caribbean, including Puerto Rico, are also affected. Some countries are reporting higher-than-usual numbers of dengue cases, including Bolivia, Colombia, Samoa, Tonga, New Caledonia, Cambodia, Malaysia, Vietnam, the Maldives, Sri Lanka and Kenya. Travelers should review up-to-date, country-specific travel information for guidance on dengue risk and prevention measures at least four to six weeks before traveling. For current travel health information and guidance, visit the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s travel website. Anyone planning to travel to or who has recently visited an area with dengue risk may be at risk for infection. The CDC advises travelers to take standard precautions when visiting such areas. These include using an Environmental Protection Agency-registered insect repellent, wearing long-sleeved shirts and long pants outdoors, and sleeping in air-conditioned rooms, rooms with window screens or under insecticide-treated bed nets. Travelers returning from areas with dengue risk should take precautions to prevent mosquito bites for three weeks. If dengue symptoms develop within two weeks of returning, travelers should seek medical evaluation. Symptoms of dengue can range from mild to severe and include fever, nausea, vomiting, rash and body aches. Symptoms typically last two to seven days. While severe illness can occur, most people recover within a week. Individuals who have recently traveled and are experiencing these symptoms should contact their healthcare provider. Healthcare providers and individuals who suspect dengue infection are advised to call the Disease Reporting Line at 808-586-4586. In areas with suspected or confirmed dengue cases, DOH personnel from the Vector Control Branch conduct inspections and mosquito-reduction activities. Reducing mosquito populations lowers the risk of dengue transmission to others. In areas without reported dengue cases, eliminating mosquito breeding sites around the home is an important preventive measure. Mosquitoes need only small amounts of standing water to breed. Common breeding sites include buckets, water-catching plants such as bromeliads, small containers, planters, rain barrels and even cups left outside. Prevent standing water from collecting around homes and workplaces by emptying containers and other items where mosquitoes can lay eggs. The latest case comes a little over five weeks after the sixth case was reported, bringing the total in the state to seven so far this year. Health officials say the individual was exposed to the virus while traveling internationally in a region where dengue is common, and that no connections to prior cases have been found. Teams have been deployed to implement mosquito-control measures in the affected area, which DOH did not disclose. “Due to the circumstances of this case, the expected risk of transmission is low,” said DOH in a news release. “However, with recent flooding from Tropical Cyclone Lala and anticipated rain in the forecast, this case is a reminder for the public to eliminate standing water as much as possible. Reducing standing water helps prevent mosquito breeding and can reduce the risk of local transmission of vector-borne diseases.” To date, there have been five cases on Oahu, one on Maui, and one on Kauai. Dengue, a viral illness spread through the bite of a mosquito, is a year-round risk in many parts of the world, including the tropical and subtropical areas of Central and South America; Asia; the Middle East; Africa; Puerto Rico; American Samoa, Micronesia, the Marshall Islands and Palau. content: newsinfo / Headlines Headlines Baguio eyes mosquito bacteria to curb dengue Technology using Wolbachia to inhibit virus from multiplying inside Aedes aegypti mosquito shows promising results in other countries By: Vincent Cabreza - Reporter / @Inquirer_Baguio Philippine Daily Inquirer / 04:35 AM August 19, 2026 TAKING ACTION City health workers conduct dengue prevention activities in Tacloban as cases rise. In Baguio, where dengue cases are also increasing, health officials are exploring Wolbachia technology as another tool to prevent mosquitoes from transmitting the virus. —Tacloban City Health Office BAGUIO CITY, Philippines —The city is being considered a pilot site for a technology that uses the naturally occurring Wolbachia bacteria to prevent mosquitoes from transmitting dengue, as cities including Tacloban intensify efforts to contain rising infections. The city council was told Monday that two companies that invested in applications of this research have expressed interest in using the city as a model site for the technology before potentially expanding it to other parts of the country. Baguio chief epidemiologist Dr. Donabel Tubera Panes said the city government participated in the Philippine Wolbachia Dialogue on June 23, where disease experts and representatives of companies discussed the bacteria’s potential in dengue control. Article continues after this advertisement Wolbachia, an intracellular bacterium found naturally in many insects, can inhibit the dengue virus from multiplying inside the Aedes aegypti mosquito, the primary vector of dengue. She said the technology has shown promising results in countries that have adopted it. In Australia, where Wolbachia has been introduced into mosquito populations for about 15 years, dengue cases declined by 77 percent and hospitalizations by 86 percent, Panes said. The bacteria is not genetically modified and does not harm humans, she said. Article continues after this advertisement Baguio has recorded 543 dengue cases since January. Data dating back to 2005 show that infections in the city tend to spike every two to three years, with health officials expecting this year’s cases to peak around mid-August before tapering off by mid-October. “Dengue is here to stay,” Panes said, adding that the experience of countries, such as Indonesia, Singapore and Australia, suggests that Wolbachia could be “the missing link in our dengue management.” Article continues after this advertisement Surveillance In Tacloban City, health authorities have intensified dengue surveillance and prevention after cases reached 272 as of Aug. 8, up 31 percent from the 208 cases recorded during the same period last year. City Health Officer Dr. Jaime Opinion Jr. said the increase prompted the city to place its public health response under a code blue alert, allowing health authorities to strengthen disease surveillance, prevention measures and preparedness. “While the increase in dengue cases in the city is alarming compared with the same period last year, it is not alarming to the point of an emergency because we have not recorded any deaths,” Opinion said. He attributed the rise partly to Tacloban’s pattern of experiencing higher dengue cases every three years, as well as inadequate water supply and changing weather conditions. “We are feeling the effects of El Niño, with periods of heavy rain followed by extreme heat. The lack of water supply also contributes because residents tend to store rainwater in containers, which can become breeding places for mosquitoes that transmit dengue,” Opinion said. With assistance from the City Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office, the City Health Office has been conducting fogging operations in barangays where dengue clustering has been reported or where at least two cases have been recorded. Health personnel are also conducting antidengue spraying in homes, particularly in dark and poorly ventilated areas where mosquitoes may hide. Opinion said hospitals in Tacloban had also admitted 374 dengue patients from outside the city, indicating that local health facilities are serving patients from neighboring provinces. Community effort Across the Cordillera region, the Department of Health recorded 4,436 dengue cases from Jan. 4 to Aug. 8. Cases increased by 9 percent in Abra, 23 percent in Benguet, 34 percent in Kalinga and 44 percent in Ifugao. Dengue is transmitted mainly through bites from infected Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes, which commonly breed in stagnant water found in discarded containers, tires, cans and uncovered water storage vessels. Opinion urged residents to regularly inspect and clean their homes and surroundings and eliminate areas where water can accumulate. Residents were also advised to wear long-sleeved clothing, use mosquito repellents and install screens or mosquito nets where possible. Early consultation is encouraged when symptoms develop. content: by PERPETUA ETYANG Friday August 7, 2026 Image generated with AI The United States has issued a travel health alert for Kenya following a rise in dengue fever cases, urging travellers to take extra precautions against mosquito bites. In a health alert issued by the US Embassy in Nairobi, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) listed Kenya among countries reporting a higher number of dengue cases in its updated Travel Health Notice. The advisory identifies Kenya's coastal region, as well as Wajir and Garissa counties, as areas where travellers should exercise caution. "Dengue is a mosquito-borne virus common in tropical and subtropical climates that can lead to fever, aches and pains, nausea, and rashes," the embassy said. The embassy urged travellers to consult the CDC's travel health advisories before travelling to affected areas and to take measures to avoid mosquito bites. Recommended precautions include using an Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)-registered insect repellent, wearing long-sleeved shirts and long trousers when outdoors, and sleeping in air-conditioned rooms or rooms fitted with window screens. The alert comes as health authorities continue to monitor dengue infections in several parts of the country, with the disease primarily transmitted through the bite of infected Aedes mosquitoes. The US Embassy advised travellers seeking more information to consult the CDC's travel health guidance or contact the agency directly before visiting affected areas. Dengue is a viral infection that affects millions of people worldwide and is transmitted through the bite of infected mosquitoes. Once diagnosed, it is important to follow medical advice closely, monitor symptoms, and prioritise rest. Adequate hydration plays a crucial role in preventing complications, while nutritious meals help support the body's recovery process. Patients should remain alert to warning signs that may indicate worsening illness and seek immediate medical assistance when necessary. In some cases, hospitalisation may be recommended to ensure close monitoring and appropriate treatment during the recovery period. In May, Garissa county embarked on a massive fumigation exercise aimed at containing the spread of dengue fever following a recent outbreak that has seen several residents hospitalised at the Garissa County Referral Hospital. The two-week exercise, which officially kicked off on Thursday, will involve public health officials fumigating drainage areas, public institutions, schools, markets and other public spaces across Garissa township in an effort to eliminate mosquitoes responsible for spreading the disease. Health officials said samples taken from patients admitted at the Garissa County Referral Hospital confirmed infections of dengue fever, a viral disease transmitted by the Aedes mosquito, which commonly breeds in stagnant water. Speaking to the press after overseeing the launch of the fumigation exercise, Hassan Abdullahi, who was representing the Medical Officer of Health said laboratory tests conducted at the National Public Health Laboratory confirmed the outbreak after 28 out of 40 samples collected from both public and private health facilities tested positive for dengue fever

The Ministry of Health and Wellness reminds the public that the rainy season increases the risk of dengue transmission. Dengue is spread by the Aedes aegypti mosquito, which breeds in stagnant water commonly found in containers around homes and communities. Dengue can cause mild to severe illness and, in some cases, can be fatal. Common symptoms of dengue include high fever, severe headache, pain behind the eyes, muscle and joint pain, skin rash, and, in severe cases, bleeding or difficulty breathing. The Ministry urges residents to seek medical attention immediately if you are experiencing symptoms. Dengue prevention is a shared responsibility. Checking homes, yards, workplaces, and communities for mosquito breeding sites can significantly reduce the risk of dengue transmission. Residents should take the following preventive measures: • Empty, cover, or remove containers that collect water around homes and businesses. • Remove discarded containers, tires, bottles, cans, and other items that can collect rainwater. • Keep drains, yards, vacant lots, and surroundings free of excessive vegetation, garbage, and debris. • Use mosquito repellents as directed. • Wear long-sleeved clothing, particularly during the early morning and late afternoon when mosquitoes are most active. • Ensure doors and windows are properly screened to prevent mosquito entry. The Ministry of Health and Wellness continues to work closely with communities, local authorities, and partners to strengthen surveillance and vector control activities throughout the country. Subscribe Health News Florida Mosquito control ramps up as dengue fever cases rise in Hillsborough and Pinellas WUSF | By Nancy Guan Published August 14, 2026 at 4:50 AM EDT Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Listen • 1:02 Nancy Guan / WUSF Mosquitoes caught in special traps are taken to a lab, where they're frozen and killed. The females, which transmit disease, are separated and sent to a lab that tests for dengue. Eight people in Hillsborough and two in Pinellas recently contracted the mosquito-borne illness locally, officials say. Both counties are under alerts. The disease is not endemic to the Tampa Bay region. The Tampa Bay region is experiencing more locally acquired cases of dengue fever than usual this year. The Florida Department of Health reported eight cases in Hillsborough County and two in Pinellas County so far, and both are on a mosquito-borne illness alert. For Pinellas, it's the first case of locally acquired dengue in over 15 years, according to data from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. "Pinellas doesn't have any modern history of having dengue in the county," said Alyssa Berro, the county's mosquito control manager. "So this is one of those cases [where] somebody has returned from somewhere they got bit. And then got bit by our mosquitoes, which then started the transmission in this area." Symptoms of dengue typically appear 15 days after being bitten by an infected mosquito. The illness, also referred to as bone-break fever, can come with joint and muscle pain. Other symptoms include pain behind the eyes, nausea, vomiting and rash. Local versus travel-associated Dengue is not what experts call endemic – or regularly found – in Florida. Typically, people will contract dengue while traveling to other countries, rather than getting bit by an infected mosquito in the Tampa Bay area. Dengue is not contagious between humans, but it can spread if a mosquito bites someone with the illness and becomes a carrier. ALSO READ: Locally acquired cases of mosquito-borne dengue reported in Palm Beach, Miami-Dade The insect can then spread the disease by biting others or breeding more dengue-carrying mosquitos. Between 2010 to 2025, Hillsborough County reported 277 dengue cases due to travel and nine locally acquired cases. The eight locally acquired cases this year were reported within the last two weeks. "And that's what makes this such a big change, is that it is going around in the mosquitoes in our county," said Gabriela Henderson, community relations coordinator for Hillsborough County Mosquito Management. WUSF file A female Aedes aegypti mosquito, the primary spreader of dengue fever, feeds on a human. Mosquito treatment Efforts to control the spread are underway. Mosquito control for both counties are treating areas by truck and helicopter aerial sprays. Pinellas and Hillsborough residents can check which neighborhoods have been treated online. ALSO READ: Before you swat that mosquito this summer, take a picture of it Technicians are also visiting homes and businesses to treat mosquito-prone areas by hand. County health officials are encouraging residents to remove any standing water around their homes. "They like to lay their eggs near humans in things like buckets, toys we might leave outside in the rain, tarps, planters," said Henderson. "Anything that can hold even just a bottle cap-sized amount of water is enough for mosquitoes to go through their whole life cycle." Henderson said tires are a common breeding ground for mosquitos since they tend to hold water. Nancy Guan / WUSF The BG trap is one type of mosquito trap being used to catch adult mosquitoes. The mosquito control teams also manage a number of mosquito traps across each county. These BG traps – or biogent traps – have components that mimic human scent and emit carbon dioxide to lure in adult mosquitos. The trapped mosquitos are then taken back to the lab, where they're frozen and killed. The female mosquitoes, which are the only mosquitoes that bite humans and animals, are separated and sent to a lab that tests for dengue. Henderson said one mosquito from Hillsborough has come back positive. Protect yourself The breed of mosquitoes carrying dengue is the Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus. These dengue-carrying mosquitoes will bite during the daytime, not just in the evening, and tend to stay low to the ground. That makes them harder to avoid and detect. Berro said homeowners should check their yards once a week for standing water. She recommended people wear light-colored clothing that covers the legs and arms when they go outside, and to use insect repellent approved by the Environment Protection Agency that contains DEET, IR3535, picaridin or oil of lemon eucalyptus. "We call those the three D's: to dump, dress and defend," said Berro. content: ROANOKE, Va. ( WFXR ) - Dengue virus is a mosquito-borne illness that is normally found within tropical and sub-tropical areas. “Dengue viruses are spread to people through the bites of infected Aedes species mosquitoes,” says Dr. Julia Murphy, the State Public Health Veterinarian for the Virginia Department of Health. Mosquitos are considered vectors, meaning they’re organisms that can transmit diseases like dengue. “The one that spreads dengue the most efficiently and is considered the primary vector, if you will, of dengue virus is called Aedes Aegypti .” The species is native to Africa, but has appeared in the U.S. sporadically over the years as an invasive species. But, the U.S. is home to another species of Aedes mosquito; Aedes Albopictus. “The kind of Aedes mosquito that we have in abundance, is one that is a competent vector, you could say, but it's really not the main driver of dengue,” says Murphy. “It has a tendency to have a broader array of animals that it bites.” According to the World Health Organization, up to 400 million people around the world are at risk of becoming infected with dengue each year. Stopping the spread of vector-borne disease But unlike other viruses that spread from person to person, dengue spreads through mosquito bites. “You have a person who's infected with dengue, a person for whom dengue virus is circulating in their blood, a mosquito vector mosquito bites that person, “says Murphy. “Then after a relatively short period of time, that mosquito becomes infected with the dengue virus, and then if that mosquito bites another person, then that person gets infected.” Earlier this month, VDH confirmed the first case of dengue to be locally acquired here in Virginia. “We had a person in Northern Virginia who tested positive for the dengue virus and it appears that that infection was locally acquired, which means that person got infected in Virginia,” says Murphy. However, health officials say while this case is historic, it’s not unprecedented. “Over the years, 2010 through 2025, of all of the dengue virus infections that were reported as happening in people in the United States about 95% of them were travel associated,” says Murphy. VDH says while other potentially locally acquired cases are possible, it’s unlikely to see other cases at this time. Rabies: A closer look at the ‘deadliest disease’ “A lot of times that people at highest risk for additional transmission are folks in the household or folks who are in close proximity to a person with dengue virus in circulation,” says Murphy. Not everyone will have a reaction to the virus, as some people can appear asymptomatic to the infection. “Dengue can have a wide clinical spectrum that can occur,” says Murphy. “A lot of people don't become sick at all.” However, for those that are impacted by the disease, symptoms can vary. “Oftentimes they'll get a fever, that's a real hallmark of dengue,” says Murphy. “Then they have general aches and pains, sort of especially one feature of dengue can be in some people, a lot of pain behind the eyes, what's called retro ball pain.” Other symptoms can include nausea, vomiting, muscle and joint pain, and a skin rash. “A smaller subset, probably around five-percent of people, can get what's called severe dengue,” says Murphy. “As the name would suggest, that is a severe illness that can result in things like shock and internal bleeding.” But while the risk of dengue spreading in the Commonwealth isn’t large, there are other mosquito-borne illnesses to be on the lookout for, including West Nile Virus. VDH says prevention is key, and there are plenty of tools people can use to not only help prevent dengue, but all mosquito-born illnesses. Back-to-school health, getting students ready for the school year “Some good prevention measures include things like when you're outdoors using mosquito repellent,” says Murphy. “What I would say is always follow the directions on the label.” Not every repellant is able to be used by all people, which is why experts say it’s important to know what ingredients are inside before spraying it on yourself, a child, or a pet. “It's important to look at that label and also look at the concentrations of of the various ingredients, because there are some precautions and recommendations for children,” says Murphy. “There may also be some cautions and recommendations associated with any pets you have.” Dr. Murphy suggests checking out the EPA’s website to determine which insect repellant is right for you. Another thing to utilize for protection is making sure you have screens on your windows, and that there aren’t any holes in them. “A lot of people like to have their door open or their windows open,” says Murphy. “Make sure that screen is in good repair, make sure your window screens are being repaired because you want to try to keep mosquitoes out.” Finally, it’s important to manage pools of water near your home, as stagnant water can become a breeding ground for mosquito larva. “You can help to drive down the populations of mosquitoes in and around your yard by helping to eliminate or routinely refreshing any standing water in your backyard,” says Murphy. Mosquito eggs need just seven to ten days to transition into a full-grown adult mosquito. “So if mosquitoes are laying their eggs in there and you're disrupting that cycle at least once a week, it'll really decrease the likelihood that any eggs that are in there would go on to become adults,” says Murphy. content_title: Army receives 2,900 dengue vaccine doses for troops
content: The Royal Thai Army Medical Department has received 2,900 dengue vaccine doses for personnel serving in areas at high risk of outbreaks and those considered at risk of developing severe dengue. The vaccines were donated by the Medical Association of Thailand under Royal Patronage at a ceremony at the Army Medical Department Headquarters on August 5, 2026. Prof Dr Keerati Chareancholvanich, president of the Medical Association of Thailand, led the association’s delegation, while Lt Gen Kriengchai Prasongsukarn, chief of the Royal Thai Army Medical Department, presided over the ceremony. The association provided the vaccines because some Army personnel face increased exposure while carrying out duties in areas where dengue outbreaks are considered a high risk. The Army Medical Department noted that dengue can occur throughout the year. Although the Army already allocates funding and maintains prevention and control measures, military working environments can make it difficult for personnel to avoid Aedes mosquitoes , which transmit the disease. The donated vaccines will be distributed to Army personnel and officials in areas experiencing outbreaks, supporting existing public-health measures intended to reduce the risk of dengue among troops

content: Manila Bulletin Environment and Sustainability Clean water and waste management are key to fighting dengue Environment and Sustainability Clean water and waste management are key to fighting dengue By Henrylito D. Tacio Dengue is hyper-endemic in the Philippines. The World Health Organization (WHO) has observed cyclical increases in dengue cases, with significant outbreaks occurring every three to five years. The World Health Organization's warning signs for dengue. So, what does dengue have to do with the environment? Water, discarded plastic bottles, and poorly managed surroundings are part of the answer. Water serves a dual purpose in the context of dengue. Stagnant water facilitates mosquito reproduction, while adequate hydration is essential for patients recovering from the disease. According to the We Are Water Foundation, dengue is spread by Aedes mosquitoes, which deposit their eggs in clean, stagnant water found in artificial containers such as buckets, flower pots, and discarded items that collect rainwater. These breeding sites can be found around homes and communities. Poor water storage practices can increase the number of mosquito breeding sites and, consequently, the risk of dengue outbreaks. An Aedes mosquito, which can transmit dengue, rests on a surface. (Photo by Henrylito Tacio) Before the rainy season, the country also experiences intense heat. Many Filipinos store water in containers such as pails and barrels. When these containers are left uncovered and are not regularly emptied and cleaned, they can become breeding grounds for mosquitoes that transmit dengue. Managing outdoor water in shared spaces and routinely emptying or covering containers are important preventive measures to reduce mosquito populations. The same concern applies to discarded plastic waste. Plastic bottles, bags, sachets, food containers and wrappers can collect rainwater and become artificial catchments for stagnant water. Poorly managed plastic waste is particularly hazardous because even small containers can retain enough water for mosquito breeding. Discarded bottle caps and other small objects can also serve as breeding sites. Aedes mosquitoes are highly adapted to human environments and tend to stay close to people. The accumulation of plastic waste around residences, roadsides, and urban areas therefore creates numerous small water reservoirs where mosquitoes can breed. Poor waste management can also affect drainage systems. Discarded plastics can clog gutters and municipal drainage, resulting in localized flooding and stagnant water. This can create additional breeding sites throughout communities, particularly during the rainy season. The eggs of Aedes mosquitoes can also survive for months under dry conditions. When breeding sites are filled with water again, some eggs can hatch, allowing the mosquito population to increase. Children are among those most vulnerable to severe dengue. (Photo courtesy of Dr. Richard Mata) For people who contract dengue, adequate hydration is also important, particularly because the disease can cause fluid loss through fever, vomiting and plasma leakage. Water and oral rehydration solutions may help maintain fluid levels, while patients with severe dengue may require medical attention and intravenous fluids. The fight against dengue, therefore, is not only a health concern. It is also an environmental and community responsibility. Keeping surroundings clean, properly storing water, removing containers that can collect rainwater, and ensuring that drainage systems remain clear are simple measures, but they can reduce the places where mosquitoes breed. During the rainy season, dengue prevention efforts begin not only in hospitals and health centers but also in homes, streets, and communities. Preventing stagnant water and managing waste properly remain among the most practical ways to make the environment less favorable for dengue-carrying mosquitoes. close Manila Bulletin Weather Producer-20260819-09:03 CANCEL NEXT VIDEO play_arrow volume_mute AD % buffered 00:00 00:00 00:38 Powered by GliaStudios Related Tags Dengue waste management dengue cases Philippines

Doctor explains Dengue fever is finally coming down, but why can this be the most dangerous phase of the illness? Doctor explains Aadya Jha / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Aug 16, 2026, 20:00 IST Share AA +Text Size Small Medium Large Follow us 1/7 Doctor explains what is the most dangerous phase of Dengue fever A falling fever usually feels like good news. After several days of high temperature, body pain, weakness and poor appetite, seeing the thermometer return towards normal can bring a family a much-needed sense of relief. But dengue does not always follow that familiar pattern of illness getting better as the fever disappears. In fact, the period when the fever starts settling can be one of the most important points in the illness. This is when some patients enter the critical phase, a short window in which dengue can suddenly become serious. Dr Ajay Nair, Sr. Consultant - Internal Medicine, Narayana Hospital, Jaipur, explained, “When dengue fever finally starts to fall, families often breathe a sigh of relief. But a drop in temperature does not always mean the danger is over. In fact, for some patients, this is when the critical phase of dengue can begin.” 2/7 The fever is falling, but something else may be changing Dengue usually moves through three broad phases: febrile, critical and recovery. The first is the febrile phase, when the patient has the familiar high fever, headache, muscle and joint pain, nausea or vomiting and sometimes a rash. Fever commonly lasts two to seven days. Then comes the part that can confuse families. The temperature may come down. The patient may even appear more comfortable. Yet, in some cases, the blood vessels are becoming more permeable. This can allow plasma, the liquid portion of blood, to move out of the bloodstream and into surrounding tissues. The process is known as plasma leakage. The problem is not simply that fluid has moved into another part of the body. Significant leakage can reduce the amount of fluid circulating inside the blood vessels. If the loss becomes substantial, blood pressure and circulation can fall, potentially causing dengue shock. That is why a normal-looking thermometer can sometimes give a false sense of security. 3/7 why does the danger appear when the fever goes away? The connection between falling fever and rising risk may sound strange, but it makes sense when dengue is viewed as a changing illness rather than simply a fever. During the febrile phase, the high temperature is often the symptom that gets the most attention. Once it drops, the family may assume the infection is ending. But around defervescence, the medical term for the period when fever settles, some patients enter the critical phase. The increased permeability of blood vessels can cause plasma leakage during this window. The CDC describes the critical phase as beginning at defervescence and typically lasting 24 to 48 hours. Most patients improve, but those who develop substantial plasma leakage can deteriorate within hours. This is also why the phrase “the fever has gone, so the dengue is gone” can be dangerous. The illness may still need close observation even though the most obvious symptom has disappeared. Dr Nair explained, “Dengue generally has three phases: febrile, critical, and recovery. The critical phase often happens around the time the fever goes down, usually between days 3 and 7 of illness, though the timing can vary. During this period, some patients can develop complications even after appearing to improve.” Most people with dengue do recover without developing severe disease. The concern is identifying the smaller group whose condition begins changing quickly. 4/7 Platelets matter, but they do not tell the whole story One of the most common things families watch during dengue is the platelet count. That number is important, but it should not become the only measure of whether a patient is safe. Platelets can fall during dengue, particularly around the critical phase. However, a low platelet count by itself does not automatically mean that a person has severe dengue. Similarly, a platelet count that has not fallen dramatically does not completely rule out a developing complication. Doctors look at the entire clinical picture. Blood pressure, pulse, urine output, hydration, fluid balance, haematocrit and changes in blood-test results can all provide important clues. A doctor may also look for evidence of fluid accumulation and assess how alert and comfortable the patient appears. There is a practical lesson here for families: do not judge recovery by one blood-test number. A patient with dengue is more than a platelet count on a report. 5/7 These are the signs that should never be brushed aside The hours after the fever settles deserve attention, particularly if the patient develops new symptoms instead of steadily improving. Dr Nair said, “The warning signs families should know are severe abdominal pain, ongoing vomiting, bleeding from the nose or gums, blood in vomit or stool, unusual drowsiness or restlessness, difficulty breathing, cold or clammy skin, and reduced urine output.” These are not symptoms to watch casually at home. Reduced urine output also matters because it can signal that the circulation and fluid balance are becoming abnormal. Difficulty breathing can occur when fluid accumulates around the lungs or when the patient's condition becomes more severe. A person who was eating, drinking and talking normally in the morning but becomes unusually sleepy, restless, breathless or cold later in the day needs medical assessment. Dengue can change quickly, so waiting for the next routine blood test may not always be appropriate. 6/7 What families should do when the fever starts falling The safest approach is not to panic when the fever drops, but also not to celebrate too early. The patient should continue following the treating doctor's advice during this period. Fluid intake, urine output, symptoms and overall behaviour need attention. Doctors may recommend repeat blood tests or clinical reviews depending on the patient's condition. Medication choices also matter. Dr Nair said, “Patients should also avoid self-medicating with aspirin or drugs like ibuprofen, which can increase bleeding risk. Paracetamol is usually preferred for fever, under proper medical advice.” It is also important not to assume that more fluids are always better. Dengue treatment requires careful attention to fluid balance. During the recovery phase, leaked fluid moves back into the bloodstream. Excessive or poorly timed fluid administration can therefore create problems, including fluid overload. The WHO dengue guideline specifically warns about this risk. Once the critical phase passes without major complications, the recovery phase generally begins. Appetite and overall well-being improve, urine output increases and the body's fluid balance gradually stabilises. Platelets may recover later than some other blood parameters, so improvement should again be judged as a whole rather than by one number. Dr Nair summed up the central message clearly: “The good news is that most dengue infections do not advance to severe dengue. Once the critical phase is over, patients enter recovery and typically start to improve.” So, when the fever falls, the thermometer should not be the only thing being checked. Watch the person, not just the number. A calmer patient with improving appetite, adequate urine output and no warning signs is reassuring. A patient whose fever has fallen but who develops severe abdominal pain, repeated vomiting, bleeding, breathing difficulty, unusual drowsiness, cold skin or reduced urine output needs prompt medical attention. With dengue, the disappearance of fever can mark improvement. But for some patients, it can also mark the beginning of the most closely watched 24 to 48 hours of the illness. 7/7 Medical experts consulted This article includes expert inputs shared with TOI Health by: Dr Ajay Nair, Sr. Consultant - Internal Medicine, Narayana Hospital, Jaipur. Doctor explains Aadya Jha | TIMESOFINDIA.COM | Last updated on - Aug 16, 2026, 20:00 IST Comments Share Continue On App 1/7 Doctor explains what is the most dangerous phase of Dengue fever A falling fever usually feels like good news. After several days of high temperature, body pain, weakness and poor appetite, seeing the thermometer return towards normal can bring a family a much-needed sense of relief. But dengue does not always follow that familiar pattern of illness getting better as the fever disappears. In fact, the period when the fever starts settling can be one of the most important points in the illness. This is when some patients enter the critical phase, a short window in which dengue can suddenly become serious. Dr Ajay Nair, Sr. Consultant - Internal Medicine, Narayana Hospital, Jaipur, explained, “When dengue fever finally starts to fall, families often breathe a sigh of relief. But a drop in temperature does not always mean the danger is over. In fact, for some patients, this is when the critical phase of dengue can begin.” 2/7 The fever is falling, but something else may be changing Dengue usually moves through three broad phases: febrile, critical and recovery. The first is the febrile phase, when the patient has the familiar high fever, headache, muscle and joint pain, nausea or vomiting and sometimes a rash. Fever commonly lasts two to seven days. Then comes the part that can confuse families. The temperature may come down. The patient may even appear more comfortable. Yet, in some cases, the blood vessels are becoming more permeable. This can allow plasma, the liquid portion of blood, to move out of the bloodstream and into surrounding tissues. The process is known as plasma leakage. The problem is not simply that fluid has moved into another part of the body. Significant leakage can reduce the amount of fluid circulating inside the blood vessels. If the loss becomes substantial, blood pressure and circulation can fall, potentially causing dengue shock. That is why a normal-looking thermometer can sometimes give a false sense of security. 3/7 why does the danger appear when the fever goes away? The connection between falling fever and rising risk may sound strange, but it makes sense when dengue is viewed as a changing illness rather than simply a fever. During the febrile phase, the high temperature is often the symptom that gets the most attention. Once it drops, the family may assume the infection is ending. But around defervescence, the medical term for the period when fever settles, some patients enter the critical phase. The increased permeability of blood vessels can cause plasma leakage during this window. The CDC describes the critical phase as beginning at defervescence and typically lasting 24 to 48 hours. Most patients improve, but those who develop substantial plasma leakage can deteriorate within hours. This is also why the phrase “the fever has gone, so the dengue is gone” can be dangerous. The illness may still need close observation even though the most obvious symptom has disappeared. Dr Nair explained, “Dengue generally has three phases: febrile, critical, and recovery. The critical phase often happens around the time the fever goes down, usually between days 3 and 7 of illness, though the timing can vary. During this period, some patients can develop complications even after appearing to improve.” Most people with dengue do recover without developing severe disease. The concern is identifying the smaller group whose condition begins changing quickly. 4/7 Platelets matter, but they do not tell the whole story One of the most common things families watch during dengue is the platelet count. That number is important, but it should not become the only measure of whether a patient is safe. Platelets can fall during dengue, particularly around the critical phase. However, a low platelet count by itself does not automatically mean that a person has severe dengue. Similarly, a platelet count that has not fallen dramatically does not completely rule out a developing complication. Doctors look at the entire clinical picture. Blood pressure, pulse, urine output, hydration, fluid balance, haematocrit and changes in blood-test results can all provide important clues. A doctor may also look for evidence of fluid accumulation and assess how alert and comfortable the patient appears. There is a practical lesson here for families: do not judge recovery by one blood-test number. A patient with dengue is more than a platelet count on a report. 5/7 These are the signs that should never be brushed aside The hours after the fever settles deserve attention, particularly if the patient develops new symptoms instead of steadily improving. Dr Nair said, “The warning signs families should know are severe abdominal pain, ongoing vomiting, bleeding from the nose or gums, blood in vomit or stool, unusual drowsiness or restlessness, difficulty breathing, cold or clammy skin, and reduced urine output.” These are not symptoms to watch casually at home. Reduced urine output also matters because it can signal that the circulation and fluid balance are becoming abnormal. Difficulty breathing can occur when fluid accumulates around the lungs or when the patient's condition becomes more severe. A person who was eating, drinking and talking normally in the morning but becomes unusually sleepy, restless, breathless or cold later in the day needs medical assessment. Dengue can change quickly, so waiting for the next routine blood test may not always be appropriate. 6/7 What families should do when the fever starts falling The safest approach is not to panic when the fever drops, but also not to celebrate too early. The patient should continue following the treating doctor's advice during this period. Fluid intake, urine output, symptoms and overall behaviour need attention. Doctors may recommend repeat blood tests or clinical reviews depending on the patient's condition. Medication choices also matter. Dr Nair said, “Patients should also avoid self-medicating with aspirin or drugs like ibuprofen, which can increase bleeding risk. Paracetamol is usually preferred for fever, under proper medical advice.” It is also important not to assume that more fluids are always better. Dengue treatment requires careful attention to fluid balance. During the recovery phase, leaked fluid moves back into the bloodstream. Excessive or poorly timed fluid administration can therefore create problems, including fluid overload. The WHO dengue guideline specifically warns about this risk. Once the critical phase passes without major complications, the recovery phase generally begins. Appetite and overall well-being improve, urine output increases and the body's fluid balance gradually stabilises. Platelets may recover later than some other blood parameters, so improvement should again be judged as a whole rather than by one number. Dr Nair summed up the central message clearly: “The good news is that most dengue infections do not advance to severe dengue. Once the critical phase is over, patients enter recovery and typically start to improve.” So, when the fever falls, the thermometer should not be the only thing being checked. Watch the person, not just the number. A calmer patient with improving appetite, adequate urine output and no warning signs is reassuring. A patient whose fever has fallen but who develops severe abdominal pain, repeated vomiting, bleeding, breathing difficulty, unusual drowsiness, cold skin or reduced urine output needs prompt medical attention. With dengue, the disappearance of fever can mark improvement. But for some patients, it can also mark the beginning of the most closely watched 24 to 48 hours of the illness. 7/7 Medical experts consulted This article includes expert inputs shared with TOI Health by: Dr Ajay Nair, Sr. Consultant - Internal Medicine, Narayana Hospital, Jaipur. 什么是登革热 “登革”一词,来源于西班牙语“dengue”。直到1869年伦敦皇家内科学院将此病定名为“登革热”,一直沿用至今。 登革热(Dengue fever)是由登革病毒(Dengue virus,DENV)经蚊媒传播引起的急性虫媒传染病。它的传播速度快,发病率高,是目前世界上分布最广、发病人数最多、危害最大的重要虫媒病毒传染病之一,在我国属于乙类传染病。 我国登革热高发季节为夏秋季,一般自每年5月开始逐渐增多,8—10月为发病高峰期。 登革热的传播和症状特点如何 登革病毒存在于登革热感染者或隐性感染者的血液中,主要经白纹伊蚊和埃及伊蚊(俗称“花蚊子”)传播。雌性伊蚊叮咬携带病毒的感染者后,病毒就会在蚊子体内大量复制,伊蚊再叮咬其他人时病毒就会被传播。传播途径主要是“感染者→伊蚊→其他人”,一般不会在人与人之间直接传播。 人体感染登革病毒后,潜伏期一般为1~14天,多为5~9天。 登革热的典型症状如下: 1.热 首发症状多为突发高热(40°C以上)伴畏寒,通常持续5~8天。 2.痛 头痛、眼眶痛、肌肉和骨关节剧烈酸痛。 3.红 面、颈、胸部潮红。 4.疹 分布于头面部或四肢躯干,为充血性皮疹或点状出血疹。 5.其他 腹痛腹泻等胃肠道症状;皮下或黏膜出血、牙龈出血、鼻衄等;白细胞计数和血小板减少;严重者甚至出现休克或多脏器功能损伤。 可通过体格检查、实验室检查(血常规、血清学检查)和影像学检查(CT、B超、磁共振),结合流行病学史和临床表现来判断和诊断。 旅游出行如何防控 1.在外应穿着长袖衣服及长裤,并使用驱蚊液,预防蚊子叮咬。 2.酒店、民宿房间应关好纱门、纱窗,房间可以使用蚊香、灭蚊气雾剂等,尤其要注意婴儿床和婴儿车,也要装置蚊帐。 3.在家中使用杀虫剂灭蚊时,要按照产品的说明进行操作,避免儿童接触。 4.避免在树阴、草丛、凉亭等户外阴暗处逗留。 5.如果出现发烧、皮疹等疑似症状,应及时就诊并主动说明被叮咬的情况。 家居日常如何防控 1.家里安装纱门纱窗和使用蚊帐,适时使用防蚊液、蚊香、电蚊拍、杀虫喷雾剂等进行驱蚊。 2.避免在蚊虫出没频繁的时段(上午7—9点和下午4—6点)在树阴、草丛、凉亭等户外阴暗处逗留,出门穿着浅色长袖衣服及长裤。 3.定期清除家居环境积水,及时清理饮料罐、食品盒、玻璃瓶等小容器垃圾,排清可能孳生蚊虫的积水。 登革热作为一种气候敏感的虫媒传染病具有明显的季节性,它属于自限性疾病,1~2周左右可恢复,并发症不常见,病死率较低,一般无后遗症。做好防蚊措施,避免蚊虫叮咬是预防登革热的最佳方式。 来源丨广东疾控微信公众号 一审丨萧渝桦 二审丨罗燕英 三审丨林伟志 创文: 觉得不错,请点这里↓↓↓ 特别声明:以上内容(如有图片或视频亦包括在内)为自媒体平台“网易号”用户上传并发布,本平台仅提供信息存储服务。 Notice: The content above (including the pictures and videos if any) is uploaded and posted by a user of NetEase Hao, which is a social media platform and only provides information storage services. 关闭 注册|手机发跟贴 登录并发贴 网友评论仅供其表达个人看法,并不表明网易立场。 目前没有热门跟贴 目前没有跟贴,欢迎你发表观点 查看更多跟贴 去跟贴广场看看 /阅读下一篇/ 返回网易首页 下载网易新闻客户端 相关推荐 热点推荐 速看!预防基孔肯雅热和登革热,从夏季防蚊开始 龙川发布 2026-08-19 14:55:29 0 跟贴 0 柳城县多措并举做好这项工作 柳城人柳城事 2026-08-19 17:03:47 0 跟贴 0 东莞体彩开展虫媒传染病防控专项排查整治 新快报新闻 2026-08-19 08:25:26 1 跟贴 1 存在多项重大事故隐患 中央考核巡查组在内蒙古多地明查暗访 央视新闻客户端 2026-08-19 13:47:00 23 跟贴 23 北京多措并举织密夏季防蚊“防护网” 北青网-北京青年报 2026-08-19 09:44:02 0 跟贴 0 北京千余家社区、公园和单位参与“无蚊害社区”建设 新京报 2026-08-19 13:25:07 1 跟贴 1 “最近几乎每天都有”!北京多区接警量翻倍,一旦直接接触立即就医!
